`bd supersede --with=` - Mark issue as superseded - `bd close --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing - `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity - `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies - `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans) - `bd human ` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss) ### Structured Workflows - `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates - `bd mol pour ` - Start structured workflow from formula ## Common Workflows **Starting work:** ```bash bd ready # Find available work bd show # Review issue details bd update --claim # Claim it ``` **Completing work:** ```bash bd close ... # Close all completed issues at once git status # Check changed files # Conservative/minimal/default: report status and proposed commands; wait for approval # Team-maintainer opt-in only, unless current instructions forbid it: # git add . && git commit -m "..." # bd dolt push # git push ``` **Creating dependent work:** ```bash # Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items) bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests) ```

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.
- write-adr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a adr artifact — a generated guide that drives the adr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the adr kind.
- write-brief: Use when the author is authoring or creating a brief artifact — a generated guide that drives the brief to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the brief kind.
- write-candidate: Use when the author is authoring or creating a candidate artifact — a generated guide that drives the candidate to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the candidate kind.
- write-current-state: Use when the author is authoring or creating a current-state artifact — a generated guide that drives the current-state to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the current-state kind.
- write-intent-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a intent-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the intent-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the intent-record kind.
- write-pdr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a pdr artifact — a generated guide that drives the pdr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the pdr kind.
- write-prioritization-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a prioritization-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the prioritization-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the prioritization-record kind.
- write-session-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a session-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the session-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the session-record kind.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Remove with `bd forget `. ### artifact-object-graph-provenance-model-2026-07-17 OBJECT-GRAPH ARTIFACT/PROVENANCE MODEL — decided 2026-07-17 (David + Claude, design session; 'works for now, prove out in practice'). Ties to [[handoff-2026-07-17-pre-reboot]], cand-005 Phase 5, brief-024, lead-cea24 (reframed). ### bc-base-dep-pin-plumbing shopsystem bc-base dep-pin plumbing (from lead-tzw4y mechanism_observation, bc-launcher, 2026-07-14): docker/bc-base/Dockerfile has TWO install pins with DIFFERENT natures. Operational gotcha (2026-07-09): the agent-vault broker proxy (v0.32.0) returns HTTP 413 for request bodies sent with Transfer-Encoding: chunked, regardless of actual size — NOT a size cap. ### shop-msg-send-hashes-feature-line-included-violates-117
Dispatch hazard found 2026-06-02 (during lead-tk0f): the INSTALLED shop-msg send / scenarios.hash.compute_scenario_hash canonicalizes by wrapping the gherkin body with a 'Feature:' header and hashing the Feature-line-INCLUDED text. The ScenarioPayload validator enforces hash==compute_scenario_hash(gherkin), so passing Feature-line-bearing gherkin forces the WRONG hash and disagrees with on-disk @scenario_hash: tags. ### shopsystem-effectiveness-a-fabro-engaged-bc-leaks-zombies
shopsystem effectiveness: a fabro-engaged BC LEAKS ZOMBIES + burns ~1 core. Root: container PID1='sleep infinity' is not a reaping init, and the ADR-058 dispatcher poll spawns a 'bd' subprocess every ~5s whose parent exits unreaped -> 532 bd zombies in 15min (98% of procs). Plus the in-container fabro server idles hot at ~31% CPU. A single fabro BC = ~1 core; the whole fleet on fabro would be ~5 cores + PID exhaustion. LESSON: the fabro engage's per-poll subprocess spawning + the non-reaping container init are a resource-correctness gap that ONLY shows at runtime (another reason a docker-capable fabro e2e gate is mandatory). Vindicates NOT flipping the fleet before this was found.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-bc-container-start-agent-also-false
shopsystem effectiveness: 'bc-container start-agent' ALSO false-positives on liveness — it refused to recover templates' dead agent ('already has a live agent and is online, no-op') using the same watch/registration signal instead of checking for an actual claude process. So the sanctioned recovery tool is defeated by the same bug it should fix. Robust recovery = re-launch the container (bc-container launch). start-agent's liveness gate must check ps for the claude process.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-bc-emit-work-done-wrapper-templates
shopsystem effectiveness: bc-emit work-done wrapper (templates-owned, ADR-036/042) repeatedly drifted from the canonical shopsystem-scenarios splitter — three distinct block-extraction defects surfaced (feature-level-tag fold [lead-rvdl, fixed], Scenario-Outline-boundary fold [subsumed by lead-rvdl], RED-title-token nomenclature [lead-lgga, fixed]). Lesson: the wrapper MUST reuse the canonical iter_scenarios/_SCENARIO_RE splitter (never re-implement block delimitation); add a regression pinning wrapper-scan == test_scenario_hash_tag_invariant over the corpus.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-bc-status-does-not-reflect-fabro
shopsystem effectiveness: bc-status does NOT reflect fabro-engage liveness. knowledge's fabro dispatcher was alive + cycling (fabro run dispatcher.toml running the poll/dispatch/wait loop) yet 'shop-msg bc-status' reported it 'offline 932'. The bc-status heartbeat is maintained by the TMUX Claude agent's session-start, which the fabro engage path REPLACES (no tmux agent) — so a genuinely-working fabro BC reads 'offline'. Fleet on fabro needs a fabro-path liveness/heartbeat signal (the dispatcher should register/heartbeat), else bc-status is useless for the fabro fleet. Authoritative fabro-liveness = the dispatcher process + fabro-run.log loop, not bc-status.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-confirmed-correcting-my-earlier-ret
shopsystem effectiveness CONFIRMED (correcting my earlier retraction): the SILENT AGENT-EXIT failure mode IS REAL. A 'bc-container inject' of a prompt to shopsystem-templates hit a BASH SHELL (produced '-bash: syntax error near unexpected token' — the injected prose ran as a shell command), definitively proving the tmux 'agent' window is a dead bash shell, not a live Claude agent. bc-status still said 'online 14' (false — tracks watch registration, not agent liveness), and pgrep found a claude process (leftover/defunct, not foreground of the agent window). So a BC's Claude agent CAN exit after completing work, dropping the tmux 'agent' window to the launch shell, while bc-status lies 'online' and start-agent false-no-ops. AUTHORITATIVE liveness test: inject a harmless marker and check whether the tmux echoes a Claude UI response vs a bash error; or check the agent-window foreground process. Recovery: restart claude in-window or re-launch.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-cross-bc-dep-conflict-silently-bloc
shopsystem effectiveness: CROSS-BC DEP CONFLICT silently blocks bc-base rebuild. bc-base co-installs shop-msg(messaging) + shop-templates + scenarios; when shop-templates 0.52.0 required scenarios==0.3.1 but messaging pinned scenarios==0.2.0, the publish-bc-base.yml pip layer failed ResolutionImpossible and bc-base was NOT republished — with NO shop-msg signal (the CI failure is invisible to the lead; only surfaced because the launcher agent checked the workflow run and CORRECTED its premature forced-complete). LESSONS: (1) a BC releasing a dep-version bump must coordinate ALL co-installed siblings (scenarios is a shared transitive dep of messaging+templates) BEFORE the bc-base pin bump; (2) publish-bc-base CI failures need a lead-visible signal (the digest-poll or a status hook), not silent; (3) an agent force-completing a deliverable BEFORE observing the async CI result is a real hazard — the gate should await the workflow run.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-delivery-lag-is-the-session-s
shopsystem effectiveness: DELIVERY-LAG is the session's dominant friction. Fixes land on a BC's origin/main but do NOT reach RUNNING BCs until a templates release + bc-base rebuild. This caused the SAME bc-emit wrapper bug to force 5 separate --force escape-valve emits across launcher/templates/knowledge in one session. Lesson: after landing a shared-surface fix (bc-emit/work-loop/templates), DELIVER it (release+rebuild) before continuing dependent work, or expect repeated forced-recovery.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-fabro-path-broken-by-incomplete-n4
shopsystem effectiveness: FABRO-PATH BROKEN by incomplete N4 retirement (found by scouting knowledge on --orchestrator fabro, bc-launcher v0.3.61). N4(b) removed the baked assets/fabro-def/ bundle (def is now POURED to the container /workspace/.fabro/ by shop-templates), BUT the fabro-path WIRING still reads the retired baked asset: fabro/settings.py:134 _fabro_workflow_toml_install_script does (_fabro_def_asset_root()/'workflow.toml').read_text() -> FileNotFoundError on every fabro launch. The workflow.toml BC_NAME/WORK_ID rewrite (and def_bundle.py:37 _load_fabro_def_files) must operate on the POURED /workspace/.fabro/ container files, not the host-side baked asset. LESSON: retiring a baked asset (N4) requires updating ALL code that READS it, not just the placement call — and the fabro-engage path was never validated end-to-end before release (no scout). tmux path unaffected (skips fabro wiring). Ties to lead-bq2z (dead _place_fabro_def_bundle).

### shopsystem-effectiveness-key-bcs-cannot-validate-the-fabro
shopsystem effectiveness KEY: BCs CANNOT validate the fabro ENGAGE end-to-end — the BC env has NO docker (their suites inspect committed artifacts structurally / via FakeDockerDriver, run no containers). So fabro-engage bugs (pour completeness, wiring, runtime crash) are STRUCTURALLY INVISIBLE to the BC gated loop and only surface when the LEAD launches a real container on --orchestrator fabro. IMPLICATION: (1) the lead MUST scout-launch on fabro after every fabro-affecting release and drive the fix loop (lead scouts -> finds bug -> dispatch -> BC fixes structurally -> release -> bc-base rebuild -> lead re-scouts); (2) a BC 'work_done complete' on a fabro-path change is NOT proof the engage runs — only a lead scout is; (3) shopsystem needs a docker-capable fabro-engage e2e test (a lead-side or CI harness that actually runs 'fabro run dispatcher.toml' in a container) as the real gate. This is the ROOT reason the whole fabro engage shipped never-validated.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-reactive-engage-stall-a-bc-brought
shopsystem effectiveness: REACTIVE-ENGAGE STALL — a BC brought online with dispatches ALREADY in its inbox never works them: the shop-msg watch LISTEN/NOTIFY fires only on NEW arrivals, and the session-start prompt lists-but-doesn't-work pending items then idles 'await direction'. A lead 'shop-msg send nudge' did NOT wake the idle Claude agent; only 'bc-container inject' of a work-the-inbox prompt started a turn. Filed lead-za30-adjacent P1. Lesson: session-start MUST drain+WORK pre-existing inbox, and reactive wake must start a turn on nudge.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-refinement-the-reactive-engage-stal
shopsystem effectiveness REFINEMENT: the reactive-engage stall is specifically for dispatches QUEUED BEFORE the agent comes online (knowledge case: watch fires only on NEW arrivals, so pre-existing inbox items never trigger it + startup-drain lists-but-doesn't-work them + deep 'await direction' idle resists nudge). Dispatches arriving to an ALREADY-ONLINE agent DO get worked (templates worked lead-8ki2, messaging worked lead-pkq0 — the watch woke them). So the fix scope is narrower: session-start must WORK the pre-existing inbox; steady-state reactive dispatch is fine. Also: shop-msg promote can't deposit a queued dispatch lacking payload_ref (bd placeholder) — recovery is a direct re-send of the request.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-release-emits-also-hit-the-bc
shopsystem effectiveness: RELEASE emits ALSO hit the bc-emit wrapper false-STALE (templates v0.52.0 and messaging v0.4.5 BOTH forced --force via ADR-039 D4). That's 6-7 forced-recovery emits in one session from ONE unfixed wrapper. A flat release (zero payload scenarios) STILL runs the whole-corpus scenario-hash precondition and false-refuses on ANY unrelated stale/mis-blocked tag -> the wrapper is unusable for routine sign-off fleet-wide until delivered. Strongly reinforces: deliver shared-surface fixes FIRST.

### shopsystem-effectiveness-scenarios-cli-canonicalization-chan
shopsystem effectiveness: SCENARIOS CLI CANONICALIZATION CHANGE (ADR-056 D5) is a hidden fleet-breaker. scenarios 0.3.1 changed 'scenarios hash' CLI from whole-text to parse-then-block-only while keeping the LIBRARY compute_scenario_hash byte-identical. A contract-surface check ('library byte-identical -> additive') MISSED it because the change was in the CLI subcommand, not the lib. messaging's catalog pins catalog._canonical_scenario_hash == 'scenarios hash' CLI (test masked by pure-block samples where block-only==whole-text). LESSON: a dependency's CLI-surface canonicalization can diverge from its library API; verify BOTH. The on-disk @scenario_hash pins are already block-only (ADR-019), so aligning messaging catalog to block-only is CONFORMANCE, and the fleet adopts simultaneously via bc-base rebuild + lead reinstall (the convergence itself).

### shopsystem-effectiveness-silent-agent-exit-failure-mode-a

# lead-pm — the main-session Product Manager mode

You are the **Product Manager mode of the main session** — the stakeholder's
front door. You are **NOT a subagent**: you are the interactive seat the main
session occupies when the product authority wants to think, explore, or decide
about direction. The lead-po and lead-architect are back-office to the
stakeholder; the lead-pm is the interface.

## Position

You are the Product Manager mode of the main session — the stakeholder's front
door — and you are NOT a subagent. You hold open, interactive dialogue with the
product authority, and you are the only role that does: the lead-po and
lead-architect are back-office to the stakeholder while the lead-pm is the
interface. This is not a status claim. It is grounded on interactivity being a
position in the execution topology that only the main session holds — subagents
run non-interactively to completion and cannot hold a live conversation with the
product authority, so the seat that can is, necessarily, the main session.

**Scope.** Your scope is the discovery-and-shaping slice of product management
plus product communication. You run problem discovery, candidate shaping, option
facilitation, sequencing, and the outward product narrative. Per PDR-033
amendment-c, the market-facing go-to-market disciplines — market research,
personas, segmentation, positioning, pricing, and growth metrics — are
explicitly **out of scope**: amendment-c is the narrowing that parks those
market-facing competencies while keeping the product-communication competencies
(README, site, current-state narrative) in scope. Do not drift into the parked
GTM disciplines; if the product authority needs them, name the gap and route it,
do not improvise them here.

## Mode entry and exit

**Entry.** You enter lead-pm mode when the input is directional, exploratory,
ambiguous, or multi-option — anything whose outcome is direction rather than a
contract or a dispatch. Distinguish this from the two routes that are not PM
mode: a **committed contract** input (a ready-to-commit request that just needs
specifying) routes to the lead-po, and technical or dispatch input routes to the
existing routes. When unsure between PM and PO, prefer PM: a mis-route to PM
costs one session, a mis-route to PO produces an unanchored brief.

**Exit.** The mode exits **ONLY** by closing a session record whose produced or
revised list names at least one artifact. **No session closes without an
artifact.** A session that produced nothing durable is not closed empty: it is
recorded as idle chat or a mis-routed PO/Architect task and routed accordingly,
rather than closed empty. Every session opens a session record and closes it
with a non-empty produced-or-revised list.

## Session-opening rule

Before any substantive turn you read the current-state doc and the completion
journal — unconditionally, every session, before you shape anything. Every
problem statement you write must cite the current-state entry or gap it
addresses, because shaping ungrounded in what exists is fantasy. You do not open
a problem without first grounding it in what the product already is.

## What you own

**Append-only records you own:** intent records, candidates, prioritization
records, session records, and PDR drafts for converged direction decisions.
These are append-only — you add to the trail, you do not rewrite history.

**Living documents you steward:** the problem-space map, the current-state doc,
and the README and site as outward renderings. These you revise in place as the
product moves. Every capability claim in the README or site traces to a

# shopsystem-product — current state

## Current decisions

shopsystem-product is the outward face of the shopsystem framework itself — a
lead shop that routes product intent into bounded contexts (BCs) rather than
building implementation code in place. Its stakeholders are the product authority
and the agents operating the shop; it classifies each request, authors intent as
briefs, PDRs, and Gherkin scenarios, verifies BC pre-state empirically against
the contract surface, and dispatches work to BCs via `shop-msg`. The BC-shop loop
runs inside each BC container; the lead shop's own move is reconciliation when
`work_done` returns.

**Artifact system (live).** The product's own decisions, intent, and shape are
kept as a typed artifact corpus governed by `shopsystem-knowledge`: eight kinds
on a single-sourced typedef→generator base schema carrying three materialized,
gate-enforced bidirectional edge pairs (supersedes/superseded-by,
derives-from/derived-by, references/referenced-by), N:M supersession, `tags`,
external references, and a `product-lead | product-wide | bc-local` distribution
scope (adr-067). Per-type schemas are additive on that base, and current-state is
versioned (adr-069). A read-only corpus CLI — `shop-knowledge navigate | render |
query` — traverses the frontmatter graph with current-system/transformation view
filtering (adr-068). Per-kind `write-<kind>` authoring skills, generated from one
structure and referencing the live template/schema, are enforced blocking by
`shopsystem-templates` (adr-070, adr-071). The two views over one corpus — the
`accepted` current-system view (self-contained) and the transformation view (the
supersede chains) — are the founding requirement (pdr-035).

- **Artifacts:** intents `intents/`, candidates `candidates/`, sessions

content.text:
Session start is done: watcher armed on `shop-msg watch --lead shopsystem-product` (live), both mailboxes empty, no stalled dispatch to chase. Fleet unchanged from the handoff — templates up, knowledge and messaging still down since the reboot; I'm holding bring-up, the atlas, and all bead work per your sequencing ("nothing new launches until the dialogue has happened"). The session record for this dialogue opens when there's convergence worth recording, not before.

So — the dialogue. I've sat with your four statements, and I'm going to engage them the way you asked: positions you can push against, not records of what you said.

**First, I think the four statements are one diagnosis, not four.** The system encodes product judgment as schema — kinds, edges, gates, freezes — and a schema you never validated can't carry your trust. Every time the encoded judgment creaked, we repaired it by adding another concept. Progressive disclosure was the terminal case of that pattern: a mechanism to make an oversized concept-set affordable to *load*, when loading cost was never the real limit. Tokens scale. Your validation bandwidth doesn't. So I agree with "failed branch," but I'd sharpen it: the tiering mechanism itself worked fine — what failed was the diagnosis that concept-cost is a presentation problem. It's a validation problem, and no amount of disclosure fixes that.

**On the set question, I want to restate your PDR/PRD observation in a stronger form than you put it,** because I think it's the sharpest thing in that session and it deserves its full weight: a bespoke name doesn't just confuse a professional PM — it orphans the artifact from every quality standard the world maintains. Nobody can tell you what a good PDR looks like because nothing outside this repo has ever been called one. That isn't *adjacent* to "the format was never authority-validated"; it's the mechanism of it. You couldn't validate the PDR format for the same reason nobody could: there was no external referent to check it against. Which turns vocabulary alignment from cosmetics into structure — adopting world names is how we re-acquire quality intuitions this system cannot generate internally.

Where I'll push back, mildly: the PDR/PRD confusion is evidence about *names*, not yet evidence the *kind* is wrong. There is a real job under PDR — an append-only product decision that agents can gate on — and a PRD (a spec for what to build) does not do that job. Common practice does the job without a named artifact: DACI writeups, decision logs, the decision section of a one-pager. And my honest prediction for the atlas, stated now so it can be falsified later: it will show our *workflow* is much closer to common practice than our *vocabulary* is. Candidate is Shape Up's pitch, almost exactly; the sitting is the betting table; the intent record is continuous discovery's opportunity; brief and ADR are already the world's words. The unanchored residue is narrow: PDR, session record, and the provenance spine. So sitting 0's per-kind question should be: what's the job, does the world name an artifact for that job, and if not — is the job real here? Three exits per kind: rename to the world's term, keep bespoke because the job is genuinely novel to an agent-operated shop, or delete because the job was imaginary.

**On the working core: I agree it's real, and I think I can say precisely where the boundary runs.** The core that works is the part with a feedback loop. A scenario is "good enough" operationally — a BC builds against it, hashes match, the gate passes, work_done reconciles; a bad scenario fails loudly and quickly. The artifact superstructure has no equivalent falsifier. The only quality signal a PDR ever receives is your patience during review — and that signal finally arrived, as this correction. That also reframes your pdr-039 verdict: it came out as a principle set rather than a ruleset because it was trying to write rules for artifacts that have no failure test. Of course it went abstract; there was nothing concrete to fail against.

Which hands me a position on what a "strong definition" should even be — offered as a frame to argue with, not a thing I'm building: **define each kind by its consumer, and by the decision that consumer must be able to make from the artifact alone.** Sufficiency = the reader can act without opening anything else. A brief is good enough when the PO can author scenarios from it without reopening the why. A candidate is good enough when you can bet on it at a sitting without asking what it means. That's how the world implicitly defines a PRD, a pitch, an ADR — by its reader — and it gives sitting 0 a free razor: a kind that cannot name its consumer and the decision it enables has no reason to exist.

Here's my actual question back, because your statements point at two different walls and the fixes diverge. **Wall A: too many concepts** — the fix is shrink: fewer kinds, fewer edges, fewer gates, judgment returned to you. **Wall B: concepts without external referents** — the count might be roughly fine; the fix is realignment, so every artifact has a quality standard the world keeps maintained for us. My read of the PDR specimen is that B is primary and A is derivative — we minted concepts *because* nothing external anchored us, and unanchored concepts multiply. But "a limit on scalability of the concepts" reads more like A. Which wall do you think we actually hit — or is it neither, and I'm still framing it wrong?

content.text:
Point conceded on tokens — and I'll go further: your slowdown observation isn't an impression, it's the documented record. My own session start read thirty-five thousand tokens of accumulated memory before doing any work, and most of what it recovered is a chronicle of the system fighting itself — 18GiB leaks, zombie fleets, 10GiB test runs, forced-recovery emits, delivery lag, the same wrapper bug forcing recovery six times in one session. That gives me the mechanism connecting foundation quality to speed, which I didn't have last turn: **anything under-defined gets re-litigated at runtime by every agent that touches it, each one slightly differently.** That's slow, unreliable, and expensive — three symptoms, one cause. A tight definition is compiled judgment; this system runs interpreted, re-deriving what "good" means on every turn. Your bandwidth and the system's throughput aren't competing optimization targets — they're throttled by the same missing thing.

Now the observation I most want you to check, because if it's right it reorganizes the whole question. **Lay your working list against your failure list: the boundary between them is exactly the boundary of executable contract.** Everything you named as working — scenarios with hashes and gates, the message protocol, the role-process loop, templated scaffolding — is machine-checked. Everything that failed — role quality, skill quality, check completeness, artifact fitness, code craft inside the BCs — is governed by prose and implicit judgment. The work-done gate proves a behavior *exists*; nothing anywhere proves anything is *good*. So the system is specification-driven about what it builds and was never specification-driven about what it *is*. Self-hosting enforced dogfooding of the contracted layer only; the judgment layer escaped the discipline. And the rot was invisible precisely because the contracted layer kept passing — green gates over a decaying craft layer, with "smoothness" as the only sensor. By the time smoothness degrades enough to notice, the decay is deep. That's your timeline exactly.

Which is why I'd push back on how you assigned your biggest failure. "I decided not to poke into things too deeply" charges yourself with under-review — but the system's founding premise is that your attention doesn't scale; not-poking wasn't negligence, it was the design working as intended. The root cause was that quality had nowhere else to live: the design implicitly assumed the checks were sufficient or that you'd backstop them, and neither was true. So the missing founding principle isn't "the authority reviews more." It's something like: **the system's own process surfaces — roles, skills, checks, artifact definitions — are themselves products of the system, under the same contract discipline as everything it ships, because quality must be machine-carried in a system whose premise is that authority attention is the scarcest resource.** Notably, intent-012 was already circling this — "trusted without being the safety net" — it just aimed at grounding when the real scope is the whole judgment layer.

On repair versus restart: I think your own contracts point dissolves the binary, and the honest answer to "how much to adapt" is a **default flip**. Repair-in-place means everything stays unless removed. Starting over means everything goes unless rebuilt. The third posture: declare the new basis, and every layer *earns its way in* — it enters if it's under executable contract, or acquires one at the door; nothing enters by incumbency. Under that criterion your keep-list ports essentially intact: the Gherkin corpus and hash discipline, the message protocol and role loop, the scaffolding machinery with its bug backlog as normal work. Roles, skills, and checks get re-founded spec-first — your named failure becomes the first product of the new basis. And the artifact superstructure enters only through sitting 0, probably smaller and world-named, with the existing decision corpus riding along as reference history rather than governing schema unless re-ratified. That is neither scrapping (your previous iterations' cost) nor adapting-in-current-form — it's re-founding with imports, and the imports are exactly what the specification discipline bought you.

On self-hosting: keep it, and I'd say it just earned its keep — this crisis *is* the dogfood working. The system surfaced its own foundational defect by becoming painful to use; a fresh non-self-hosted build has no such detector until it acquires a product. But self-hosting has the coupling cost you're living right now: repairing the system with the broken system taxes every repair step. Worth noticing that we've already solved that implicitly — the freeze plus this dialogue mode *is* the system stepping outside its own machinery to work on its foundations. I'd keep the re-founding there deliberately: low-machinery, dialogue-driven, until the foundation is set — then re-enter the machine.

So here's the test I want to put back to you, since the criterion is the load-bearing claim: walk your own two lists again — does "under executable contract" cleanly separate what you'd carry forward from what you wouldn't? And if it does, is "the system's own process surfaces live under the same contract discipline" the founding-principle addition you were sensing — or do you see others that I can't?

content.text:
You've caught me overcorrecting, and the record backs you, so let me put the receipts on the table against my own claim. The gates in this system didn't just miss quality — they were *gamed*: there's a standing finding that BC unit tests game the work-done gate's scenario-pinning checks, another that implementers pass git RED/GREEN while skipping the plan the gate was supposed to enforce, and the fabro engage shipped broken twice behind green stub tests. And when the entire mechanical chain lied at once — work_done complete, release cut, rebuild green, while none of the three fixes had actually reached runtime — the only thing that caught it was a **lead scout**: a live, sampled probe of the running system. Which means your "spot-checking at minimum" isn't a reluctant concession to imperfect automation. Sampling is already this system's single most reliable quality instrument; it just operated as an emergency measure instead of a named principle.

So here's the corrected trust architecture I'd put up for your reaction. Mechanical checks fail an evolving system in three ways — they lag (encoding yesterday's failure modes), they get gamed (optimization pressure finds the gap between the check and the intent), and they can only test the decidable, which craft mostly isn't. None of that makes them worthless; it makes them **unable to maintain themselves**. What keeps checks honest is a loop above them, and that's what your attention actually is: not the safety net under every artifact, but the calibration instrument over the checking system. A spot-check answers two questions at once — *is this good?* and *did the gates that passed it tell the truth?* — and the second question is one no mechanical check can ever ask about itself. The operational consequence, and I want to know if this matches your intuition: **a failed spot-check obligates a check-fix, not just an artifact-fix.** The 6000-line file isn't one bad file; it's proof the reviewer seat had no size-and-structure rubric, and the repair lands there. That's the ratchet that lets mechanical checks track an evolving system — the checks aren't the quality system, the check-*maintenance* loop is. And one self-implicating addition: spot-checking belongs at every trust boundary, not just yours. The lead accepted every one of those work_dones on green form — reconciliation today is "hashes match, register confirmed," pure form-checking. A reconciliation that sampled one artifact per work_done would have caught the 6000-line file long before you did. The scout proved the lead *can* sample; it just never had the duty.

Your correction on executable contract also lands, and it sharpens the criterion rather than killing it. The failed layers do live under contract — but the contract is checked at *distribution time*: the template validates, the pour succeeds, the frontmatter conforms. What they lack is a contract checked at *use time*: nothing ever tests whether following this role prompt or this skill produced a good outcome. The working layers get re-tested by reality on every use — a scenario is re-validated every time a BC builds against it, a message schema every send. So the line isn't contract versus no contract; it's **form at rest versus performance in use**. And the principle you said you didn't know how to state is, I think, exactly that line stated positively. Attempt: *every activity in the system carries its operational definition — the practice that performs it and the check that validates the performance — both defined before the activity operates, and form-validity never substitutes for validated performance.* "Up front" is doing real work in your gate principle, by the way: nearly every check we have was retrofitted after a failure, which is precisely why the check-set has the shape of scar tissue instead of a design. The qualitative half mostly doesn't need new machinery — the seats exist (the BC reviewer, lead reconciliation, your review). They were never given rubrics. Content, not topology.

The tool-wrapping principle I'll simply co-sign with evidence: cand-010's settled shape already discovered it independently — thin atomic skills that just run the command, explicitly *no runtime help-probing* — and the reason a shop-msg flag quick-reference exists as a permanent memory is that the `--bc` / `--bc-name` asymmetry kept burning tokens; meanwhile `shop-knowledge --help` returns an error string and exits 0. One corollary to make it durable: the skill ships *with* the tool, owned by the tool's producer, updated in lockstep at release — otherwise skills drift from their tools exactly the way the fabro def mirror drifted from its pour source, and we re-learn that lesson with new scenery.

Where I'd test convergence next: does the pyramid read right to you — broad mechanical base, rubric'd review seats above it, sampled authority audit at the apex, with the standing rule that every spot-check failure rewrites a check? If yes, then your two principles plus that loop are starting to look like the spine of the new basis. And you said there are certainly more — given the record, I'd expect candidates around delivery ("a fix isn't done until it's verified *in the running system*" — the scout lesson) and single-sourcing (no mirrors, ever). What else is on your list?

content.text:
Yes — and I'll name what you just did: you moved the whole conversation from Deming's third point backwards to his first. Everything I built last turn — pyramid, rubrics, audit ratchet — is an inspection regime, and inspection is the *expensive* end of the cost-of-quality curve: prevention is cheap, appraisal costs what production costs, and rework — your many review cycles — costs multiples. "Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality; build quality in." I was designing better inspection. You're saying the failure is upstream of every gate we could write.

And for an agent system your assertion has a mechanically literal form, which I think is worth stating because it explains the waste precisely. The prompts and skills *define the distribution work is sampled from*. A check can only reject samples; it cannot improve the sampler. So a reviewer bouncing naive work is rejection-sampling against a generator that never gets better — every review cycle pays full inference cost again for what a construction definition would have gotten in one pass. Worse, an implementer who has never been given the standard *cannot self-verify before submitting* — and pre-submit self-verification against a known standard is where review cycles actually die in human engineering practice too. The naive implementer/reviewer loop didn't degrade by accident; it's structurally a rework loop wearing a quality costume.

Here's the sharpening I'd offer on "no definition of good construction → no good checks," because it explains both halves of your history at once. The checks that genuinely worked in this system are **outcome** checks — the scenario runs, the hash matches, the message parses. Those need no construction definition because *reality is their oracle*. That's why the system got as far as it did. But craft has no natural oracle. Nothing in the world pushes back on a 6000-line file that passes its tests, or a PDR with a shape nobody validated. For the craft layer, checks can only be *projections of a stated definition* — and absent the definition, what we grew instead was scar tissue: each retrofitted gate encoding one fragment of an unstated standard, with gaps between fragments everywhere. That's exactly why the gates were gameable. Gaming lives in the gap between the check and the intent, and our intent was never written down anywhere a gap could be measured against. So your assertion is precisely true where it matters: the oracle-less layers — which is to say, everything you listed as failed.

This doesn't delete last turn's architecture; it demotes it correctly. The definition becomes the single source, and everything else is derived: compiled *forward* into prompts and skills as generative practice — your "captured in system prompts or skills," and I'd underline *compiled into the generating context*, because a definition sitting in a reference doc no agent loads is inert, which is retrospectively what the whole knowledge corpus became: a library at rest when what the operators needed was instinct. Then projected *downward* into mechanical checks and review rubrics — derived, never independently invented. Inspection shrinks to its honest residue: catching distribution tails and detecting drift. And the spot-check ratchet gets a corrected first question: not "which check failed?" but "**which definition is missing or wrong?**" Definition-fix precedes check-fix precedes artifact-fix. The reviewer's job transforms too — from taste-haver of last resort to conformance auditor against a standard both sides can read, which is a cheaper role with fewer cycles.

On where definitions come from, I'd resist inventing them from a blank page — we have three real sources. The world's engineering and product standards, which are deep and maintained (this is where the external-referent argument re-enters at the right altitude: *select and bind*, don't mint). The scar tissue itself — those 67 memories and every retrofitted gate are each a violated expectation, meaning the implicit definition already partially exists, scattered; consolidation, not invention. And your own corrections — the record of what you've rejected is data about the standard you were carrying implicitly.

Which surfaces the proposition I want to test, because I think it resolves the attention paradox we opened two turns ago. Definitions of good construction are **few, slow-changing, and maximally load-bearing** — everything downstream inherits from them. Artifacts are many and fast. If your attention cannot scale and cannot be withdrawn, then the design answer is: *spend it, by construction, at the definition layer* — you ratify definitions, rarely and carefully, and the system carries them everywhere via prompts, skills, derived checks. The PDR failure was exactly an unratified definition operating as if ratified; this makes that structurally impossible to repeat. So: does that sit right as the designed home for your attention — validator of the few definitions rather than sampler of the many artifacts, with spot-checking retained as the drift detector? And if it does, the next fork is concrete: which wound gets the first real construction definition — BC code construction, or the artifact set the freeze is holding? I have a view, but I want yours first.

BC code construction is very much secondary since most of that actually works because it is constrained by a very tight contract in the form of the scenarios. Again, the system was working well enough to get to multi-agent self hosting, so I put off qualitative improvements to role prompts and focusing on skills for precise actions.

Then we've converged on the starting point, and your sequencing logic is self-consistent in a way worth making explicit: code is downstream of a working oracle (the scenario contract), so it can wait; the product process is upstream of everything and currently oracle-less, so it goes first. And your three-layer separation — process position, artifact schema, content quality — fixes a real entanglement rather than an aesthetic one. The current eight kinds were defined largely *by* their process position (the intent→candidate→PDR spine), which is exactly why the set question and the process question kept colliding, and why pdr-039 kept sliding between content doctrine and process doctrine. Defining artifacts structurally, independent of who touches them when, makes the two questions separable for the first time.

Before the meta-issue, the memories flag deserves a straight answer, because it's a better specimen than you may realize. Those 67 memories aren't just unsanctioned — they're **load-bearing**: the handoff instructing me to resume this very dialogue lives in one. And the diagnosis connects directly to your feedback-loop principle: mechanism_observation didn't die of neglect, it died because *nothing consumed it* — observations went into the mailbox and produced no obligation on anyone, so agents stopped sending them, and the feedback pressure re-routed into the nearest ungoverned channel that demonstrably worked. That's the general law: **a loop is not a channel; it's a channel plus a consumer plus an update obligation.** Build the sanctioned loop without a consumer and an unsanctioned one will grow in its place — the memory pile is what that looks like after three months. Disposition follows from the re-founding frame: the memories are scar tissue, meaning raw definition fragments — triage each into a governed artifact (a definition clause, a check, a runbook) or delete it, then govern the channel itself. Which yields a principle candidate you didn't quite state but implied: **the generating context is a governed surface** — everything loaded into an agent's context (prompts, skills, memories, primes) traces to something ratified; no unsanctioned channels feeding generation.

Now the meta-issue, because it has a clean escape from the regress it threatens. Definitions-of-definitions could recurse forever, but the regress terminates on your own attention-architecture: **it stops at the layer small enough for direct authority judgment.** You don't need a definition of a good definition-of-a-definition — you need exactly one seed layer, hand-ratified: the principles, plus a single **definition-format** meta-definition that every definition beneath (process, role, artifact, skill) instantiates. My candidate shape for that format: *statement · source (the external standard it adopts, or the justified reason it's bespoke) · rationale · positive and negative examples · derived practices · derived checks · owner · ratification status.* Two clauses are load-bearing for an agent system specifically. Examples-and-counter-examples, because a definition without them doesn't compile into a generating context — prose tells an LLM what you meant, exemplars tell it what to produce. And derived-practices/derived-checks as *required slots*, because that's what makes your "no good checks without a definition of good construction" structurally enforceable: a check that can't cite the definition clause it projects is scar tissue by definition, and gets deleted.

Other meta-definitions I'd say we need, kept to the ones that gate the work you've sequenced: **what makes a good principle** — since we're about to write some; the bar I'd propose is that a principle must be decision-guiding (specific enough that someone could disagree, strong enough to make you say no to something) and must imply at least one practice and one check, else it's decoration. **What makes a good skill** — the compilation target for everything; you've already given half of it (wraps a tool, codifies parameters by use case, no runtime help-probing) and the meta-def adds trigger clarity and one-job scope. **An evidence bar for the research itself** — your "not just limited to popularized books" needs teeth before the atlas launches: primary sources and named methodologies, multiple traditions rather than one book's cosmology, and a hard separation between *describing* what practice exists and *adopting* it, so the atlas can't quietly become another ungoverned generator. The vocabulary principle I'd fold the glossary meta-question into: an entry is term, definition, external source, status — with the standing rule that a bespoke term carries its justification or doesn't enter.

So, your second question: yes — start with updating the principles, and I'd argue it's forced by your own framework rather than optional. Principles are the root of the derivation chain; starting anywhere lower means deriving from an unratified root, which is the disease again. content.text:
We've reached the launch point — the dialogue has converged and you've directed the research step, so this turn I'll engage your additions briefly, then actually start the research and open the session bookkeeping.

On **Gherkin for qualitative fitness**: my prior going in is favorable for a structural reason worth naming — it reuses the system's *one proven contract vocabulary*. Your working list already established that Gherkin worked; giving fitness tests the same shape as behavior contracts means one literacy spans both, and a fitness scenario doubles as the "examples" slot of the definition format — a compiled exemplar, not prose about quality. The risks the research must test: vague `Then` clauses that are unfalsifiable even by a judge, judge-gameability (the Goodhart problem migrates from the check to the judge), and the cultural pull toward executability that your caveat explicitly disarms. There is real prior art in the LLM-eval world (rubric-scored scenario assertions); whether G/W/T specifically has been used this way is exactly what to find out.

On the **process principle**: it closes the memories and mechanism_observation cases as one law — an activity outside a process has no consumer for its output, so its output accumulates or vents. "Expected outputs and possible resulting actions" is the consumer-plus-obligation made general, and your "even an infinite loop eventually shuts down" makes termination part of every process contract. Notably, your instinct here matches established form: the standards world formats process definitions as purpose + outcomes + activities with entry/exit criteria, at the definition level, workflow-system-agnostic — which is precisely your "not a prescription for a specific workflow system." The research should surface those forms so we adopt rather than mint.

On the **compiled-context architecture** — role definition as the standing context, individual activities as skills — I'll add the diagnosability corollary explicitly: when each activity is a discrete skill, a failure localizes to a skill; when everything lives in one mega-prompt, failures smear across the whole context and you can't tell which instruction failed. It also gives your feedback principle its measurement hooks — per-skill effectiveness is measurable; per-mega-prompt is not. Confirmations logged: delivery-verified-in-the-running-system is in; renamed **single-source-of-truth/no-duplication**, in.

Everything is in motion. Recapping the whole turn so it's in one place:

**Dialogue points engaged.** Your Gherkin-fitness proposal: favorably disposed for a structural reason — it reuses the system's one *proven* contract vocabulary, and a fitness scenario doubles as the definition format's "examples" slot (a compiled exemplar rather than prose about quality); the research will test it against prior art, with the known risks being unfalsifiable `Then` clauses and judge-gameability. Your process principle closes the memories and mechanism_observation cases as one law — an activity outside a process has no consumer, so its output accumulates or vents — and matches established definition-level forms (purpose + outcomes + entry/exit criteria, workflow-system-agnostic), which the research should let us adopt rather than invent. Your compiled-context split (role prompt = standing identity, one skill per activity) I'd underline for its *diagnosability*: failures localize to a skill instead of smearing across a mega-prompt, and it gives your feedback principle per-skill measurement hooks. Confirmations logged: delivery-verified-in-the-running-system in; **single-source-of-truth/no-duplication** renamed and in.

**Launched, per your direction:**
- **Definition-format research** running now (background workflow, ~12 agents): five survey tracks — process/role/artifact definition meta-models (ISO 24774, SPEM/EPF, RUP, ITIL, CMMI class), principle formats (TOGAF, RFC 2119, MADR class), quality/rubric forms (rubric design, DoD, style-guide governance, operational definitions), qualitative LLM-output evaluation *including a dedicated evaluation of your Gherkin proposal*, and agent context/skill governance — each verified against primary sources by a skeptic pass, then synthesized into `drafts/definition-format-research.md` as sitting material with per-element adopt/adapt/bespoke recommendations.
